question.value: Search for signatures of carbon grain (refractory organics) destruction in hot protostellar envelopes by comparing hot and warm gas components of oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor organic molecules across 37 high-mass protostars.

evidence.quote: In this work we use one such molecular surveys with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to search for the signatures of destruction of carbon grains through a two-component temperature fit to oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor organics.
We then compare the ratios of the hot number of molecules to warm number of molecules for species with and without oxygen in a sample of 37 protostellar systems.
In this work we use the publicly available ALMA data from the ALMAGAL large program (project ID: 2019.1.00195.L).

analysis_steps.goal: Compare observed ratios with an analytical spherical envelope model

method.value: Derive analytical expectation for N_hot / N_warm in a power-law spherical protostellar envelope assuming pure ice sublimation at T_sub without additional hot gas-phase chemistry, and compare with observed ratios.

evidence.quote: Here we explain what is expected for the hot and warm number of molecules from a simple analytical model.

The total number of molecules of species $i$ in the hot gas and in the warm gas can then be compared as $$\begin{equation} \frac{\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm hot}}{\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm warm}} = \frac{X_{i,\rm hot}}{X_{i,\rm warm}} \left(\frac{T_{i,\rm{hot}}}{T_{i,\rm{warm}}}\right)^{-3.75}. \label{eq:ratio} \end{equation}$$

key_parameters.value: Density power-law index p = -1.5, temperature power-law index q = -0.4, T_hot = 300 K, T_warm = 150 K

evidence.quote: Assuming a spherical model with a power-law density and temperature as a function of radius with powers $p=-1.5$ and $q=-0.4$ based on observations and radiative transfer models

Assuming $T_{\rm hot} = 300$ K and $T_{\rm warm} = 150$ K consistent with the average excitation temperatures of the hot and warm gas for the studied molecules (see Appendix 9), $(T_{i,\rm{hot}}/T_{i,\rm{warm}})^{-3.75} =0.07$.

assumptions.value: Spherical envelope with power-law density and temperature profiles, sublimation temperatures <= 100-150 K, and constant abundance X_hot / X_warm = 1 if no hot gas chemistry occurs.

evidence.quote: Therefore, if there is no additional gas phase chemistry in the hot gas (i.e., $X_{i,\rm hot}/X_{i,\rm warm} = 1$), $$\begin{equation} \frac{\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm hot}}{\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm warm}} \sim 0.1. \end{equation}$$
It is worth noting that this result is valid for molecules with sublimation temperatures of $\lesssim 100-150$ K so that there exists a warm component in the gas.

validation.value: Checked sensitivity to optically thick steeper temperature profile (q = -0.5), which changes the power from -3.75 to -3.0 and N_hot / N_warm from 0.07 to 0.13.

evidence.quote: To check how this assumption changes the calculations we take a steeper temperature profile with $q=-0.5$ for the optically thick regime (see (cite: Adams1985) for low-mass and (cite: Nazari2023Highmass) for high-mass sources). This will change the power of -3.75 to -3.0 and the value of $\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm hot}/\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm warm}$ from 0.07 to 0.13.

findings_qualitative.value: Oxygen-rich molecules (CH3OH and HNCO) systematically show no enhancement in their hot component relative to analytical expectations of simple ice sublimation.

evidence.quote: Using observations of $37$ high-mass protostars with ALMA, we find that oxygen-containing molecules (CH$_3$OH and HNCO) systematically show no enhancement in their hot component.

Our findings in Section 3 show that the mean of hot number of molecules to warm number of molecules for oxygen-rich species agrees well with the expected ratio of ${\sim} 0.1$ from the simple analytical model in Section 4.

findings_qualitative.value: Nitrogen-containing oxygen-poor molecules (CH3CN and C2H3CN) show a systematic enhancement of a factor of ~5 in their hot component, indicating additional gas-phase formation in the hot gas triggered by destruction of refractory organics.

evidence.quote: In contrast, nitrogen-containing, oxygen-poor molecules (CH$_3$CN and C$_2$H$_3$CN) systematically show an enhancement of a factor ${\sim} 5$ in their hot component, pointing to additional production of these molecules in the hot gas.
We attribute the enhancement of oxygen-poor molecules, CH$_3$CN and C$_2$H$_3$CN, in the hot gas to destruction of refractory organics and find it to be common in high-mass protostellar systems.

findings_qualitative.value: Destruction of refractory organics implies higher C/O and N/O elemental ratios in the hot gas than in the warm gas.

evidence.quote: This destruction implies a higher C/O and N/O in the hot gas than the warm gas, while, the exact values of these ratios depend on the fraction of grains that are effectively destroyed.

claims.hypothesis: Destruction of carbon- and nitrogen-rich refractory organic grains in hot protostellar gas (>=300 K) leads to top-down gas-phase production and enhancement of nitrogen-bearing, oxygen-poor organic molecules relative to oxygen-rich molecules.
claims.experiment: Fit high-upper-energy (E_up > 400 K) optically thin lines in ALMAGAL spectra of 37 high-mass protostars using CASSIS to measure hot gas molecule numbers of CH3OH, HNCO, CH3CN, and C2H3CN, and compare hot-to-warm molecule ratios against a spherical power-law envelope analytical model.
claims.result: Oxygen-rich species (CH3OH, HNCO) have mean hot-to-warm ratios of ~0.12 matching the no-chemistry analytical prediction (~0.1), whereas oxygen-poor species (CH3CN, C2H3CN) have mean ratios of 0.48 and 1.47, showing a systematic ~0.7 dex (factor of ~5) enhancement.
claims.finding: Ubiquitous destruction of refractory organics occurs in hot protostellar envelopes, enhancing oxygen-poor nitrogen-bearing molecules and raising the C/O and N/O ratios in the hot gas.

evidence.quote: Using observations of $37$ high-mass protostars with ALMA, we find that oxygen-containing molecules (CH$_3$OH and HNCO) systematically show no enhancement in their hot component.

In contrast, nitrogen-containing, oxygen-poor molecules (CH$_3$CN and C$_2$H$_3$CN) systematically show an enhancement of a factor ${\sim} 5$ in their hot component, pointing to additional production of these molecules in the hot gas.
We attribute the enhancement of oxygen-poor molecules, CH$_3$CN and C$_2$H$_3$CN, in the hot gas to destruction of refractory organics and find it to be common in high-mass protostellar systems.

why_this_data.value: The ALMAGAL survey provides high sensitivity across a large sample of 37 sources to detect both optically thin minor isotopologues (probing warm gas) and weak high-E_up (>400-500 K) lines of main isotopologues (probing hot gas).

evidence.quote: We use data from the large program ALMA Evolutionary study of High Mass Protocluster Formation in the Galaxy (ALMAGAL, PIs: S. Molinari, P. Schilke, C. Battersby, P. Ho) because of its high sensitivity to detect both optically thin minor isotopologues of the most abundant molecules such as methanol to probe the warm gas and the optically thin weak lines of the major isotopologues with $E_{\rm up} > 400-500$ K to probe the hot gas.

why_this_method.value: Fitting only E_up > 400 K lines of main isotopologues avoids optically thick low-E_up lines and isolates the hot gas component, while comparing total numbers of molecules (N_tot = A * N) eliminates dependence on the assumed emitting area.

evidence.quote: When fitting these high-$E_{\rm up}$ lines, the lines with $E_{\rm up} < 400$ K are ignored as they are usually (marginally) optically thick and even if they were not optically thick, their emission would be dominated by the warm component.

However, we stress that the relevant quantity for our study is the total number of molecules ($\mathcal{N} = A N$, where $A$ and $N$ are the emitting area and column density) which does not change if a different emitting area is used as long as the lines are optically thin.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Variations in envelope temperature power-law index (q = -0.5 instead of -0.4) or assumed fixed excitation temperature (200-500 K) were tested and rejected as explanations for the factor of ~5 difference because they alter ratios by less than a factor of 2.

evidence.quote: To test whether this assumption is valid, we varied the excitation temperature from 200 K to as high as 500 K for a few sources and found that the column densities could only change by a factor of $\lesssim2$.
This will change the power of -3.75 to -3.0 and the value of $\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm hot}/\mathcal{N}_{i, \rm warm}$ from 0.07 to 0.13.

limitations_admitted.value: Isotope ratios derived from Galactic center distance relations could introduce uncertainty if an object is an outlier.

evidence.quote: If an object is an outlier with respect to those relations, the calculated column densities from isotope ratios could have an additional uncertainty.

limitations_admitted.value: HNCO excitation temperatures are uncertain due to the lack of detected lines spanning a wide range of E_up.

evidence.quote: However, we note that these excitation temperatures are uncertain given the lack of detected lines with a large range of $E_{\rm up}$, while column densities can be measured accurately.

limitations_admitted.value: C2H3CN hot column densities are approximate and lack error bars because only one unblended line with E_up ~ 435.0 K is available and T_ex is fixed to 300 K.

evidence.loc: Measurement of hot column densities of C2H3CN
evidence.quote: Hence, we fix the temperature to 300 K and only fit the line with $E_{\rm up} \sim 435.0$ K to find an approximation for the hot column densities of C$_2$H$_3$CN. We do not measure the error bars as it is not possible to firmly measure them.

limitations_admitted.value: Higher vibrational states in the CDMS partition function for CH3CN above 300 K and CH3OH above 300 K are not included.

evidence.quote: The higher vibrational states each contribute to less than 1% at 300 K and hence are ignored here.
The vibrational levels included in the partition function are sufficient for temperatures up to 300 K.

limitations_admitted.value: The exact fraction of refractory organics destroyed and whether the trend extends to other COMs or low-mass protostars remain unknown.

evidence.quote: It is yet to be confirmed whether the trend seen in Fig. 3 holds for other oxygen-poor (e.g., C$_2$H$_5$CN) and oxygen-rich species (e.g., CH$_3$OCH$_3$).
However, the exact values of these ratios depend on the fraction of refractory organics that are destroyed in these high-temperature regions which is not known.

referee_caveats_inferred: Spectral fitting is performed using a subjective 'fit-by-eye' method rather than an automated statistical sampler (e.g., MCMC).
Spatially unresolved hot core observations blend disk and envelope components together.
Non-LTE or radiative pumping (infrared pumping of vibrational states at high temperatures) is not modeled; purely thermal excitation is assumed.
Warm C2H3CN column densities in the companion paper were derived from the main isotopologue rather than 13C isotopologues, risking optical depth effects in the warm component.
